paragraphs.source_en: The memory of this heroic age is preserved only in a few place names in Sistan. But the ruins of a grand citadel and palace atop a high basalt outcropping above what was once a shimmering lake hint at the pre- Arab splendor of the region. 42 Here, at Kuh-e-Khwazmi, only a short ride from the Afghan border and southwest of the modern village of Divaneh, were elegant and sprightly murals from the second century ad. Drawing on Buddhist, classical Greek, and Persian sources, they help us understand why the people of Sistan might later have viewed the Arabs and their allies as uncouth imposters. The capital of Sistan was the moated city of Zaranj, just over the modern border in Afghanistan, some 375 miles southeast of Nishapur.

The capital of Sistan was the moated city of Zaranj, just over the modern border in Afghanistan, some 375 miles southeast of Nishapur.

paragraphs.source_en: Surrounded by salt marshes formed by the adjacent Helmand River and protected from windblown sand by a huge barrier wall, Zaranj boasted thirteen gates and shops that extended for more than a mile along the roads leading from the center. 43 During the Arab invasion, this city became a major focus of resistance. Thereafter the locals organized themselves under the populist banner of the Karijiites, the extremist sect from southern Iraq who, as 212 • Chapter 7 we have seen, claimed that ability rather than genealogy should be the basis for worldly power in Islam. They denied the authority of the caliphs and asserted the right of armed revolt against any Muslim whom they deemed to be deviating from Muhammad’s true precepts.

They denied the authority of the caliphs and asserted the right of armed revolt against any Muslim whom they deemed to be deviating from Muhammad’s true precepts.

paragraphs.source_en: Even before the arrival in Zaranj of three brothers from the countryside, one a coppersmith, the second a mule-driver, and the third a carpenter, the Kharijites were on a roll, conquering neighboring regions and scaring the caliphs in Baghdad. The coppersmith, named Yakub ibn Laith (840–879), emerged at the head of this volunteer army, which was Hellbent on casting off the yoke of Arab rule. Since the Persian word for coppersmith is Saffar, Yakub and his dynasty came to be known as the Saffarids.
